newsitem.title: USA: Texas officials refuse to delay Mexican's execution.
newsitem.headline: Texas officials refuse to delay Mexican's execution.

text.p: A Texas parole board refused on Tuesday to halt Wednesday's scheduled execution of a condemned Mexican citizen in a case that sparked diplomatic protests from the Mexican government.

The decision was handed down as prison officials here placed the condemned man, Irineo Tristan Montoya, on a routine suicide-watch one day before he is set to die by lethal injection for his role in the 1985 murder of a Texas man.
Tristan's family, from the northern Mexican border state of Tamaulipas, issued a plea for his life.

"My son is innocent. He was cruelly deceived," Emilia Montoya, the condemned man's mother, told Mexico City's Formato 21 radio station in a telephone interview from Huntsville, where the family has gathered.

"My son was forced to sign a document 12 years ago which he thought was to authorise his deportation but which was a confession to a crime he never committed. He does not speak English; he was cruelly deceived," said Montoya, who is suffering from terminal cancer.

Despite a plea from the Mexican government, Texas Gov. George Bush said he would not delay the execution unless the courts need more time to consider eleventh-hour appeals in the case, which has attracted little notice in Texas.
The Mexican poet Octavio Paz, a Nobel Prize winner for literature, joined the clamour late Tuesday, sending a letter to Bush asking him to spare Tristan's life.

"I want to argue for clemency, I don't want to argue the law," Paz wrote, acccording to a report on the Televisa network's 24 Hours news broadcast. "One offence is not eliminated with another offence. One life is not paid for with another life."

Tristan was sentenced to die after confessing to the November 1985 murder of John Kilheffer, a Brownsville, Texas man who was stabbed at least 22 times; his body was dumped in a grapefruit grove along the Rio Grande River near the Texas-Mexico border, prosecutors said.

Tristan told police he and a friend, Juan Villavicencio, were picked up by Kilheffer while hitchhiking. Tristan said Villavicencio attacked Kilheffer after he asked the men to go to a motel to have sex with him, prosecutors said.
Tristan was convicted and sentenced to die for his role in the killing. Villavicencio was tried for capital murder and acquitted in a separate trial, prosecutors said.

The U.S. Supreme Court asked Texas prosecutors to clarify whether Tristan, a Mexican citizen, was informed of his right to speak with an official with the Mexican consulate in Texas before making a statement to police.
Tristan's court-appointed lawyer said Brownsville police apparently were unaware of Tristan's rights under the Vienna Convention, which also protects U.S. citizens abroad.
"There's no record at all that they have any clue about his rights," Dallas attorney Bonnie Goldstein said.
Goldstein filed an appeal with the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals late on Monday, alleging that a juror who condemned Tristan to die knew the victim and visited the crime scene during the trial.

Tristan is one of 12 Mexicans on death row in Texas and 36 sentenced to die for crimes committed in the United States. He would become the second Mexican executed in Texas, where Ramon Montoya, who was not related to Tristan, was put to death in March 1993 for killing a Dallas police officer.
